title: Presbyopia: age-related difficulty focusing up close
intro: Presbyopia is a gradual reduction in the eye's ability to focus on nearby objects as its natural lens becomes less flexible with age. Reading small print or looking at a phone may become harder even when distance vision seems clear. It is common, but new visual symptoms still deserve an eye examination rather than an assumption that every change is normal ageing.

sections.heading: Notice which activities have become difficult
paragraphs: You may hold a book farther away, need brighter light or develop tired eyes during close work. Explain which tasks are affected and whether the difficulty is gradual, sudden, in both eyes or mainly in one. Presbyopia is different from ordinary long-sightedness, although both can affect near vision and may occur together. It also does not explain every headache or every episode of blurred vision.

sections.heading: Arrange an examination, not just stronger readers
paragraphs: An eye-care professional can check focusing, the difference between the eyes and eye health. Bring your current glasses and explain your working distances: a phone, computer screen and fine craftwork may require different arrangements. Mention diabetes, medicines, previous eye surgery and other symptoms. Buying reading glasses may help a task, but it does not replace an examination or rule out cataract, retinal disease or other problems.

sections.heading: Choose correction for the way you use your eyes
paragraphs: Options include reading glasses, lenses that provide more than one focusing range and suitable contact lenses. The choice depends on existing prescriptions, the difference between the eyes, comfort, cost and daily tasks. Ready-made readers provide the same power in both lenses and may not suit everyone. Ask how a proposed lens works at each distance and whether you need separate glasses for particular activities. Do not assume one pair is appropriate for driving and reading.

sections.heading: Make close work easier without expecting a cure
paragraphs: Larger text, good lighting and a comfortable working distance can reduce practical difficulties. Keep the lens clean and ask for help if frames fit poorly. Presbyopia can progress, so a prescription may need review. Wearing properly chosen glasses does not mean the eyes have become dependent on them. Changes to screen settings can help access information, but cannot diagnose an eye problem or replace the optical correction you need.

sections.heading: Treat sudden symptoms as a different problem
paragraphs: Sudden loss or marked reduction of vision, a new shadow or curtain across sight, new flashes or a sudden increase in floaters require urgent eye assessment. Do not attribute them to presbyopia or wait to try stronger glasses. Severe eye pain or an eye injury also needs prompt help. For a gradual return of close-work difficulty without warning signs, arrange a routine prescription and eye-health review rather than continually guessing a lens strength.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: explaining a work task
examples.text: Someone can read a phone by holding it farther away but struggles with a computer screen. At an eye appointment, they describe both distances and their existing glasses. They ask which correction fits their tasks instead of buying a stronger pair simply because its number is higher.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: recognising an urgent change
examples.text: A person who normally uses reading glasses suddenly notices flashes and a dark shadow in one eye. They seek urgent eye assessment. They do not assume the glasses have stopped working or postpone care until their next routine appointment.

questions: Does the examination show presbyopia alone or another eye problem as well?
Which lens option suits my reading, screen work and distance-vision needs?
